result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.transitive_reduction()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the transitive reduction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L46932-L47059){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.transitive_reduction() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Transitive reduction](/assets/graphs/transitive-reduction.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A DAG on A, B, C, D: the chain A to B to C to D plus three shortcut arrows A to C, B to D and A to D, in the accent color. The reduction drops the shortcuts, shown dashed, because the chain already reaches the same nodes." width="100%"} The transitive reduction is the minimal subgraph that maintains the same reachability as the original graph. It removes redundant edges while preserving all path relationships. If there's a path from `A` to `C` via `B`, the direct edge `A -> C` (if it exists) is redundant and will be removed. This method only works on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Cyclic graphs do not have a unique transitive reduction. Time complexity: `O(V × E)` where `V` is nodes and `E` is edges Space complexity: `O(V + E)` ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New directed graph representing the transitive reduction. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on an undirected graph or a graph containing cycles. ::: ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - simplifying dependency graphs to show only direct dependencies - reducing storage for reachability queries - visualizing the minimal structure of a DAG - cleaning up inferred relationships ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The transitive reduction of a DAG is *unique* (Aho, Garey, and Ullman, 1972): among all subgraphs with the same reachability, exactly one attains the minimum edge count, and this call returns that graph. Uniqueness fails for cyclic graphs (any edge on a cycle can be removed without losing reachability), so the implementation raises `ValueError` on cyclic input rather than picking an arbitrary reduction. The construction runs in $O(V \cdot E)$ time and $O(V + E)$ space. Reductions are especially useful for visualizing the essential dependency structure of a DAG without the visual clutter of edges implied by transitivity. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The direct edge `A -> C` is redundant here because `C` is already reachable via `A -> B -> C`, so the reduction removes it: ::: {#2843bdaa .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "C"), # Redundant: A can reach C via B ] ) ) reduction = graph.transitive_reduction() # Returns 2 (A->C removed, out of the original 3 edges) reduction.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: The same idea simplifies a dependency graph down to its direct dependencies, dropping edges that are already implied by transitivity: ::: {#e0c5cde2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["app", "lib", "utils", "core"]) .add_edges( [ ("app", "lib"), ("lib", "utils"), ("utils", "core"), ("app", "core"), # Redundant (app -> lib -> utils -> core) ("lib", "core"), # Redundant (lib -> utils -> core) ] ) ) reduction = graph.transitive_reduction() # Returns 3 (down from 5), keeping only the direct dependency chain reduction.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: Because a unique transitive reduction only exists for acyclic graphs, calling this on a graph with a cycle raises an error: ::: {#e4c1e08f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "A"), # Creates a cycle ] ) ) error_message = None try: graph.transitive_reduction() except ValueError as e: # The graph contains a cycle, so no reduction is defined error_message = str(e) error_message ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 'Graph contains a cycle - not a DAG. Processed 0 of 2 nodes' ``` ::: :::
